newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Ex-Irish p.m. Haughey named in cash inquiry.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Irish p.m. Haughey named in cash inquiry.

text.p: Former Irish Prime Minister Charles Haughey was named as a recipient of more than a million pounds when an official investigation into cash payments to politicians opened in Dublin on Monday.

The counsel for the tribunal, Dennis McCullough, told an investigating judge that Haughey, one of the stars of the Irish political firmament, received 1.3 million pounds ($2 million) from businessmen Ben Dunne between 1987 and 1991. It was the first time Haughey, prime minister four times between 1979 and 1992, had been officially named in a scandal that has already claimed the scalp of one government minister and created a pre-election furore.
Michael Lowry, a rising star in the ruling Fine Gael party of Prime Minister John Bruton, quit last year when a newspaper broke the story that Dunne had paid for the renovation of his Tipperary home.
McCullough told the tribunal that Dunne would testify that he gave Lowry up to 200,000 pounds because of business relationship between Dunne's stores and a refrigeration company owned by Lowry.
In addition, Dunne paid much of the 350,000 pound bill for the renovation of Lowry's house which included the cost of "furniture, paintings and a custom-built double bed."

But media interest in the tribunal has centred on allegations that Dunne, whose family owns a department store chain, had paid cash to Haughey of the Fianna Fail party, the most powerful political force in Ireland.

McCullough, setting out the evidence the tribunal will hear, said that Haughey had approached Dunne to "help him out of financial difficulty" and that four separate payments were made through intermediaries to the former Prime Minister.
"The evidence which Mr Dunne will give is that between December 1987 and November 1991 he arranged for 1.3 million pounds to be paid to the benefit of Charles J. Haughey," he said.
McCullough said that there was no suggestion that money paid to either Haughey or Lowry or any other figures to be named in the investigation was to buy political favours.

But the news that a millionaire Irish businessman had given cash to an assortment of politicians and political parties has raised calls for a new code governing funding of political parties and more transparency.

Haughey, who has been in virtual retirement since he stepped down as Prime Minister in 1992, has said nothing publicly about the allegations, which coincide with the run-up to national elections due by November.
But Bertie Ahern, current Fianna Fail leader, moved at the weekend to distance himself from a one-time mentor who dominated Irish politics for more than a decade.

Ahern told a weekend party conference that anyone named by the tribunal should be presumed innocent until proven guilty but said he would not tolerate unethical conduct. Ahern wants the tribunal to carry out its work before Bruton calls an election so that all politicians and parties named by it will have to testify before the poll.
